item.title: Latitudinal Heterogeneity in South Asian Monsoon Changes Since the Last Glacial Maximum Revealed by Ganga–Brahmaputra Vegetation Record
item.dc:creator: Coralie Zorzi, Stéphanie Desprat, Valier Galy, Christian France‐Lanord, Αlbert Galy
item.description:
Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology — matched: last glacial maximum, insolation, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, Holocene
Abstract Future changes in South Asian climate are expected to amplify flooding and drought, yet the spatial and temporal variability of the South Asian monsoon (SAM) under different climate regimes remains poorly constrained. Here, we present a new marine pollen record from the Bay of Bengal (BoB), informing on the vegetation of the Ganges‐Brahmaputra (G‐B) River basin whose outlet via the lower Meghna lies near 21.3°–21.8°N, and compare it with bulk and leaf‐wax δ 13 C and δD, and planktonic foraminiferal δ 18 O records, all from the same site. The G‐B basin was characterized by an open landscape with sparse subtropical trees during Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 2 indicating drier and colder conditions. This is in sharp contrast with the development of tropical forests during MIS 1. During the Holocene, changes in the forest composition, characterized by a progressive increase in dry tropical trees relative to moist taxa, showed large‐scale drying, with more pronounced winter dryness after 8 ka. The comparison with the pollen records located off Mahanadi (20°N) and Godavari (18°N) catchments, both within the Indian core monsoon zone reveals that the composition of the forests differs strongly, showing a persistent north–south hydroclimate gradient. At orbital time scales, vegetation records from the western BoB support that the SAM variability is intrinsically linked to the ITCZ migration and largely affected by the Northern hemisphere ice‐sheets and insolation forcing; this is particularly significant for the Holocene. However, the spatial heterogeneity of hydroclimate conditions suggests additional modulation by Himalayan orography, and vegetation through moisture recycling.

item.title: Merging Regional Climate Models and Remote Sensing Observations to Better Estimate Mountain Snow Water Equivalent
item.dc:creator: Jack Dechow, Michael Durand, Melissa L. Wrzesien, Jessica D. Lundquist, Karl E. Rittger, Jeff Dozier, … (+2)
item.description:
Water Resources Research — matched: snowpack, data assimilation, regional climate model, reanalysis, remote sensing
Abstract Large‐scale, high‐resolution estimation of snow water equivalent (SWE) in mountainous regions remains challenging. Continental‐scale approaches, including SWE reconstruction and regional climate model (RCM) simulations, are computationally expensive at high resolutions. We present Blender, a variational data assimilation method that improves modeled SWE and snowfall time series by modifying snowpack mass and energy balance while minimizing changes to input precipitation and energy fluxes, subject to remotely sensed snow cover fraction constraints. Blender combines the advantages of RCM simulation and SWE reconstruction and can be applied as a post‐processing step to many gridded snow data sets. We tested Blender at 500 m resolution in the Tuolumne watershed, Sierra Nevada, USA, during water years 2013, 2016, and 2017 (low, average, and high snow accumulation). We tested Blender with prior inputs from an RCM and ERA5‐Land (ERA5L), and evaluated posterior (output) performance using 18 Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) flights, and compared its performance with the Western United States Snow Reanalysis (WUS‐SR). Blender improved spatial SWE patterns relative to ASO in all years for the RCM prior (RMSEP: 17.2% → 11.5%, R : 0.39 → 0.72) and ERA5L prior (RMSEP: 13.9% → 12.9%, R : 0.003 → 0.59), approaching WUS‐SR performance (RMSEP = 9.5%, R = 0.82). Blender improved snow water storage (SWS) estimates for the RCM prior but not for ERA5L prior, although ERA5L posterior SWS remained reasonably accurate (median absolute error of 27%). Blender provides a flexible and efficient pathway toward higher‐resolution, large‐scale SWE estimation in mountainous regions.

item.title: Volcanic impacts on East Asian climate since 1400: insights from climate reconstructions and paleoclimate reanalysis
item.dc:creator: Chia-Yu Chen, Wan‐Ling Tseng, Charles A. Lin, Hsin‐Cheng Huang, Kuan‐Hui Elaine Lin
item.category: Geografiska Annaler Series A Physical Geography
item.description:
Geografiska Annaler Series A Physical Geography — matched: paleoclimate, reanalysis
This study analysed volcanic impacts on East Asian temperature and precipitation (wetness/dryness) anomalies and investigated the consistency of climate responses between the REACHES reconstruction and paleoclimate reanalysis product (ModE-RA) from the 15th to 20th centuries. Volcanic events were compiled from the eruption chronology based on ice-core sulphate data, and 10 major eruption events were identified. For each event, the eruption year was designated as t0 and used as the reference year for event alignment. Superposed epoch analysis was applied with a ± 8-year window to compare post-eruption years (t = 0–8) against pre-eruption baselines (t = −8–−1) by a significance t-test. For identifying whether extreme years (percentile thresholds from the top 5%–25% in temperature and precipitation fields) are attributed to volcanic forcing or natural variability, we adopted Bayes’ conditional probabilities and applied an exact binomial test to perform reverse inference. Both datasets showed robust post-eruption cooling signals, the strongest being within t0 +3 years. Precipitation responses were controversial: REACHES revealed overall wetting, whereas ModE-RA suggested drying, indicating a consistent cooling effect of major volcanic eruptions and divergent responses in hydroclimates. Future analysis should focus on the hydroclimatic effects of volcanic eruptions using high-resolution reconstruction data and simulations.

item.title: Monthly-updated territorial fossil CO2 emissions estimates for Japan
item.dc:creator: Taro Kunimitsu, Robbie M. Andrew
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: CO2, climate change
We present a low-lag dataset of monthly CO2 emissions from fossil fuel consumption and industrial processes in Japan, derived directly from official statistical data. The monthly dataset can be used to estimate the annual emissions a year ahead of the official estimates submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Such monthly emissions estimates will provide further opportunities for understanding in a timely manner the reasons behind emissions changes, leading to targeted policy changes for climate mitigation.

item.title: Evaluating the Behavior of 230 Th and 3 He Constant‐Flux Proxies Across a Carbonate Preservation Gradient in the Cocos Ridge
item.dc:creator: Iva Tomchovska, Frank J. Pavia, William R. Gray, Patrick A. Rafter, Jess F. Adkins, William M. Berelson, … (+1)
item.description:
Global Biogeochemical Cycles — matched: proxy
Abstract We present a comparison of extraterrestrial 3 He ( 3 He ET ) and excess 230 Th ( 230 Th xs ) as constant flux proxies across a depth transect on the Cocos Ridge, evaluating their behavior as a function of carbonate dissolution and lateral sediment redistribution. Overall, 60% of paired 3 He ET ‐ and 230 Th xs ‐derived mass accumulation rate (MAR) estimates overlap within 1σ uncertainty, indicating broad agreement between the two systems. However, statistically significant discordances between He‐ and Th‐derived MARs occur in three of four cores, with He‐derived MARs exceeding Th‐derived MARs at the ridge crest (positive ΔMAR values) and falling below Th‐derived MARs at flank sites (negative ΔMAR). The discordance at the ridge crest is consistent with sediment winnowing and preferential removal of 3 He‐bearing particles, whereas the smaller discordances in flank cores are best explained by a complementary focusing signal, likely reflecting redistribution of material removed from the ridge top. Evaluation of the negative ΔMAR offsets demonstrates that 230 Th xs is effectively retained during carbonate dissolution, as ΔMAR responses remain small despite strong CaCO 3 preservation gradients, and theoretical constraints indicate negligible thorium mobility. When applied jointly, the two proxies provide complementary constraints on MARs that would remain unresolved using a single proxy. However, their interpretation remains site‐dependent, requiring careful consideration of sediment composition, transport regime, and analytical limitations. Because sedimentary burial fluxes are calculated from component concentrations and MAR, these proxy‐dependent differences directly affect estimates of carbonate and other elemental burial fluxes, with implications for reconstructing both past and modern marine biogeochemical cycles.

item.title: SeidarT: an open-source full-waveform seismic and electromagnetic wave propagation modeling toolbox demonstrated in snow and ice
item.dc:creator: Steven Bernsen, Christopher Gerbi, Senthil Vel, Knut Christianson, Seth Campbell
item.description:
The Cryosphere
We developed open-source software that simulates how elastic and electromagnetic waves travel through snow and ice with the aim to advance and make accessible ice and snow imaging methods. This helps researchers test survey designs and interpret field measurements without expensive or risky expeditions. Parameters influencing the mechanics of snow and ice are easily input from JSON files, and geometries can be generated using an image editor allowing for time effective production of models.

item.title: Hybrid implicit–explicit XFEM simulation of injection-induced seismicity: resolving multi-scale rupture nucleation and dynamics
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Sabah, Mauro Cacace, Inga Berre, Iman R. Kivi, Hannes Hofmann
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Injecting fluids underground for energy projects can trigger earthquakes. Predicting these events is difficult because underground pressure changes slowly, while faults can move in a fraction of a second. We developed a computer method that switches between two ways of calculating these processes. In our test, it reduced computing time by 62 % while giving similar estimates of earthquake size and total fault movement. Differences in the fastest movements show that further testing is needed.

item.title: Slope-Constrained Orography (SCO v1.0) for explicit discrete-slope control in terrain preprocessing: a case study with WRF-ARW (v4.6.1)
item.dc:creator: Yulong Ma, Xingwen Jiang, Lin Mu, Zhiwei Heng
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
High-resolution weather models over mountains need terrain smoothing to avoid crashing, but standard methods smooth everywhere regardless of need. We developed Slope-Constrained Orography, a tool that uses one slope-angle setting to adjust only the points that are too steep. Tested over the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, stable simulations were achieved while modifying far less terrain than standard smoothing, offering a simpler approach to running weather models over steep terrain.

item.title: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
item.dc:creator: Bernard Aumont, Richard Valorso, Andrew Rickard, Mike Jenkin, Julia Lee-Taylor, John Orlando, … (+3)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
This study presents the first open-source release of a tool that automatically generates chemical mechanisms for the atmospheric oxidation of organic compounds. Simulations for five hydrocarbons, under conditions ranging from urban to remote, are compared with a benchmark mechanism. Results show that describing successive oxidation steps is key to simulating the formation of low-volatility and water-soluble species important for aerosols. A reduced mechanism reproduces most of these results.
